title: Great Britain wins three gold medals in 28 minutes at world indoor championships
content:
Great Britain had a golden hat-trick of medals at the world indoor championships in 28 minutes on Sunday night in Torun, Poland.

Within half an hour of one another, Georgia Hunter-Bell (1500 meters), Keely Hodgkinson (800m) and Molly Caudery (pole vault) won world titles in their respective finals.

Hunter-Bell came first, crossing the line first in a British record time of three minutes and 58.53 seconds. It is the quickest run by any woman this year, and was almost an entire second faster than the rest of the field.

She held off fast finishers behind her in Jess Hull, Nikki Hiltz and Agathe Guillemot, who all broke four minutes — the world-class standard. Hull took silver in an Oceanic record of 3:59.45s and Hiltz’s 3:59.68s was a personal best, while Guillemot set a French record.

“This year I’ve developed so much as an athlete,” Hunter Bell told reporters in the mixed zone. “Mentally has been the biggest difference, believing I can win, whereas last year, I didn’t believe.”

The 32-year-old is the first British woman to win this title — with compatriot Josh Kerr winning his second 1,500m world crown on Saturday night — and it is a first gold for Hunter-Bell. She took bronze in this event last year indoors and finished fourth at the European indoor championships.

“Today I was really calm,” she said, biding her time when Ethiopian Burke Haylom pushed the pace hard from 200m in. At one stage she had a three-second lead but Hunter-Bell reeled her in as they approached the final lap.

“I had to (close), otherwise that gap was getting bigger and bigger and I was like ‘we might not catch her.’ It was a bit of a risk but you’re making these decisions in split seconds so I feel like I’m deserving (of the win),” the Brit said.

“I’m not afraid of doing that if it looks like we’re going to be in a position to medal. It was just so exciting.”

Just after she crossed the line, Caudery made the decisive clearance in the pole vault. She and Slovenian Tina Sutej had clean cards up to 4.80m, but both failed their first attempt at 4.85m. Sutej, who won bronze at the world championships in Tokyo last September, jumped before the Brit and was unsuccessful at her second attempt.

Caudery sailed over a height seven centimeters shy of her national record (4.92m), with this her biggest clearance since last August at the British championships. It provided some redemption for the 2024 world indoor champion, who missed out on the Paris Olympics final two years ago because she did not make a height in qualifying. Last September, she injured her ankle in the warm-up of the world championship final in Tokyo and was unable to compete.

“I couldn’t have dreamt of a better evening, it means more than anyone else could possibly understand,” Caudery said in the mixed zone.

She said she felt relief and it had “been a really hard two years” because she missed the chance to medal at two global championships.

“To go through that and come back, it just feels amazing. I feel like I was more confident before Paris (Olympics) than today and look what happened. So it’s just like trusting in my ability and with those journeys I’ve gained so much experience,” she added.

Caudery said that it took significant work with her coach and medical team to return to an international level. Even six weeks ago she was struggling to get off the ground in training. “Coming back from Tokyo was quite a long rehab with my ankle, then I started back jumping in January. I came back with a lot of mental difficulties. That was a lot to work through. It was run throughs and (moving up) poles to regain confidence.”

Then came Hodgkinson’s turn, the biggest gold-medal favourite of the night, having set an indoor 800m world record last month.

She ran from the front, hitting the halfway mark in 56.96s. Through the third 200m lap she gapped the field, leaving Switzerland’s Audrey Werro, American Addison Wiley and Ethiopian Nigist Getachew in a three-way scrap for the other medals, with Werro taking silver and Wiley bronze.

Hodgkinson held her form, running 28.84s over the final 200m to finish in a championship-record 1:55.31s. It was the second-quickest run ever for this distance and just half a second outside her own world record — she now holds three of the fastest five times for 800m indoors, and is sixth all-time outdoors.

This title was the only one missing from Hodgkinson’s set — she’s the Olympic and European champion from 2024 — and she becomes the first British woman to win an 800m world gold indoors or outdoors. She took bronze outdoors in Tokyo six months ago, with Hunter-Bell the silver medallist there.

“I think it’s turning into Super Sunday for us girls.” Hunter Bell said, referencing the famous Saturday afternoon of the 2012 London Olympics where Team GB won three golds. Hodgkinson, who trains with Hunter-Bell at the M11 track club in Manchester, was too nervous to watch her compatriot race.

All three embraced and celebrated with their flags on the track before fulfilling media duties, and Hodgkinson returned less than an hour later to anchor the 4x400m women’s team, who placed fifth. Her split of 50.10s was the quickest of any athlete.
